I noticed two different columns- total ratings and reviews. To my knowledge, ratings are when someone leaves a star out of 5, and reviews are when someone writes and posts something about the recipe beyond just a number. I created a column to represent the difference between these two variables, dubbed the “silent raters.” These are people who leave a number rating without saying anything in a review. Silent raters = total ratings minus reviews. The higher the silent raters, the more total ratings and the less reviews a recipe got. This scatterplot shows a trend between the variable silent ratings and the average rating of a recipe. I notice a correlation between the two variables. As the number of silent raters goes up, the score of rating for a recipe tends to increase. The opposite is also true. This makes sense, because if someone likes a recipe, they’ll give it some stars. But if someone hates a recipe, they have something to say about it, and are more likely to leave a review.

Insight #1 - Do games with longer reviews correlate with higher ratings? | Ratings seem to have no strong correlation with the length of reviews. Games of similar ratings span all level of review lengths Most long reviews are for highly reviewed games, and vice versa. | This graph indicates that review length does not indicate game quality, majority of the time.

Insight #2 - Is there a correlation between high rating and high wishlist amount? | There is a strong correlation between the quality of a game and the amount of wishlist saves it has. This indicates that high rated games may generate more buzz and conversation around them leading others to wish to buy it.

Insight #3 - Do longer summaries equate to higher reviews? | There is no strong correlation between rating and summary length. The correlation here is much less concrete than in insight #1 referring to review length. This most likely is because this is less about customer opinion and more about what the objective description of the game is. This could also indicate that game depth or complexity does not have any impact on customer satisfaction.

Insight #4 - Do games with bigger teams behind them get higher ratings? | There seems to be no strong correlation between the size of teams and the rating the game obtains. All 3 standard team sizes obtain a wide range of ratings. Although 3 has the lowest sample size, it does have the highest average rating This graph indicates that team size does not generally matter for game quality.

Insight #5 - What is the most common genre? | The most common genre combination is Adventure/RPG by a significant margin, then followed by Adventure/Platform and Adventure/Shooter. Adventure as a base genre appears consistently across nearly all top combinations, suggesting it is the dominant genre in the dataset. Pure single-genre games like just 'Shooter' or 'Adventure' alone still rank in the top 10, but most games tend to blend multiple genres together. This graph indicates that Adventure is the backbone genre of the dataset, and developers rarely release games under a single genre label.

Insight #6 - How spread out are data scores? Are some scores rarer than others? | A vast majority of video game ratings are concentrated between ~3.3+ to the 4 range. The number of ratings seem to strongly taper off when getting closer to the ~4.7 range or higher. The same can be sad for the inverse as it approaches the 3 rating range. This suggest that most users are happy with their purchases and very little have strong regrets.

Insight #7 - Has the average game rating changed over the years? | I set the dataset from 2001-20021, because of the short list of games outside those years leading to misleading ratings. The average game rating has been largely unstable. Since 2001, game ratings have seen as high as a ~3.9/5 average rating and as low as 3.5/5 average rating. This indicates that time may not have much effect on the quality or enjoyment level of games.

Insight #8 - Have games been getting more genres added to them over the years? | Genre count has steadily rose over the years. The amount of games released in each year may skew the mean but the graph still shows strong overall growth across all time periods. Though overall growth is positive, it’s not very steady seeing consistent drops as the graph moves over time. We can infer from this increase that as time passes more genres are explored and more games opt to mix and add these genres.

Insight #9 - Has the length of reviews increased over the years? | The graph shows no strong upward or downward trend in review length over time. Review lengths fluctuate consistently between roughly 160-320 words across all years, with no clear direction. The most notable spikes appear in the early 1990s and around 2000, but these may be due to fewer games being released those years, skewing the mean upward. This indicates that despite gaming communities growing significantly over time, the depth at which individual users write about games has remained largely the same.

Insight #10 - How have plays, wish lists, and backlogs changed over the years? | Plays mean has seen consistent overall growth since the mid 1980s, peaking around 2010-2011 before slightly declining. Wishlist and Backlogs mean have both grown steadily at a similar pace to each other, remaining significantly lower than plays throughout. The large gap between plays and the other two metrics suggests that as the gaming library grows, players are accumulating more games than they can realistically get through, leading to the steady rise in wishlists and backlogs alongside plays.

Anime has grown rapidly in global popularity over the past few years, reaching audiences far beyond Japan and competing with mainstream entertainment worldwide. Major titles like Demon Slayer: Kimetsu no Yaiba and Chainsaw Man have gained massive followings, and in some cases, rivaled or even outperformed popular American films at the box office and on streaming platforms. As anime continues to expand in influence, it raises interesting questions about what makes certain shows more successful, popular, or highly rated than others. To explore what makes some anime popular or highly rated, I analyzed a dataset of over 15,000 anime. The data was pulled from the Jikan API v4 endpoint/top/anime and includes info like scores, genres, episode counts, and audience engagement.

Top 10 Highest Rated Anime in the Data Set & Their Genres | Looking at the top 10 highest rated anime, all of them score very closely as you can see in the bar chart. Most of them are between 8.5 and 9, showing that they are all considered extremely high quality by viewers. Sousou no Frieren (Frieren: Beyond Journey’s End) stands slightly above the rest, but overall there isn’t a huge gap in scores, which suggests that multiple anime are seen as top-tier, not just one specific anime stands out. However, what’s more interesting is the variety in genres across these top-rated anime. While action and adventure appears quite frequently, there’s also a mix of drama, fantasy, sci-fi, and even comedy like in all of the Gintama animes. This shows that there isn’t just one “type” of anime that gets high ratings. There are different styles and genres that are all successful. For viewers, this means that sticking only to popular or trending genres might cause them to miss out on other highly rated anime that don’t get as much attention. Even though these anime are in the highly rated group, they may not all be the most popular (I will analyze this in later slides). This supports the idea that ratings and popularity don’t always match. Basically, this is encouraging viewers to look beyond the rankings and explore a wider range of anime, since some of the best-rated shows might not be the ones everyone is talking about.

Tell: This addresses question 1 about whether team size affects rating. Based on this data, team size does not seem to make too much of a difference since solo and two developer teams produce almost identical average ratings. This suggests that the quality of a game comes down to other factors beyond just how many teams made it.

Show: Most studios have made fewer than 5 games and their average ratings range widely from below 1 to above 4.5. As studios make more games the ratings tend to stabilize around 3.5 to 4.0. Shooters at the bottom doesn't mean they are bad, but it could just mean that it’s very oversaturated which will make it harder to stand out. From this insight, we can see that for indie game studios it could be a smart move to lean into genres like visual novels or turn based strategy games because not only are they cheaper to produce but they are also favored more highly by players.

The sharp drop after 2022 is probably because the dataset only captures games up to a certain point, not because fewer games are actually being made.
